questions.problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2})$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{u}{2})} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(u/2)} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}) \\ \,0\, & \,\text{ }\text{ }\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡v}{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{u}{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ 4u+6v\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y=4u+6v.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =4 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \,\text{ }4\, & \,\text{ }6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\cdot 6-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot 4 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{ln}⁡v \\ {u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have $x=u\operatorname{ln}⁡v$ and $y={u}^{2}{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\frac{u}{v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡v & \frac{u}{v} \\ 2u{v}^{2} & 2{u}^{2}v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot 2{u}^{2}v-\frac{u}{v}\cdot 2u{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}v(\operatorname{ln}⁡v-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u-5v \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=3u-5v$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(u+v).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-5 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u+v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{u+v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ \frac{1}{u+v} & \frac{1}{u+v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (\frac{1}{u+v})-(-5)\cdot (\frac{1}{u+v}) \\  & =\frac{8}{u+v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\, & \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2} \\ uv\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\frac{{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}}{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}u & -v \\ v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =u\cdot u-(-v)\cdot v \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,-2)}=(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5.
$$

For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v \\ 3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2u\operatorname{cos}⁡v$ and $y(u,v)=3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot 3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-(-2u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =6u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =6u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)}=6(1)=6.
$$

questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{v}^{2}+uv \\ v-u\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={v}^{2}+uv$ and $y(u,v)=v-u.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v+u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & 2v+u \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-(2v+u)\cdot (-1) \\  & =v+2v+u \\  & =3v+u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(8,-2)}=3(-2)+8=2.
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,1)}=-8(-2)(1)=16.

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v).$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & -\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v))-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v))\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is 

$$

questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+v \\ 2u-{v}^{3}\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 1 \\ 2 & -3{v}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-3{v}^{2})-1\cdot 2 \\  & =-6u{v}^{2}-2 \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(1,2)} & =(-6u{v}^{2}-2)\,{|}_{u=1\,v=2} \\  & =-6(1)(2)^{2}-2 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-26|\cdot \delta A \\  & =26\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ u+v\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-preserving?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ u+v\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-1\cdot u \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}v-u & >0 \\ v & >u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,2)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/928c9f7761e597884525a92388346c486c4e0df9c2c942cf31ad87164676613e.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x=(u+v)^3$ and $y=(u-v)^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =3(u+v)^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =3(u+v)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2(u-v) & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3(u+v)^{2} & 3(u+v)^{2} \\ 2(u-v) & -2(u-v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2(u-v))-3(u+v)^{2}\cdot 2(u-v) \\  & =-12(u+v)^{2}(u-v).\end{aligned}
$$

                    Evaluating a Jacobian Determinant
canonical_examples.problem:
For the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/7fc9eb28594744f04c1934d10b7e9751c9f9855897f4cc4da05b8a5e82a93f3d.svg)

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/5e056d63a91b0f4ae7dcb1c076764b862b0321b47c6e586cc91acd9e01dd36c8.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/370aba8042cc3dbd6c5c9dc15751e50dd8fe7be36d0cb220966da075bf9e2e43.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v) = 2v\cos{u}$ and $y(u,v) = v\sin{u}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u-2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot v\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =-2v({sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u) \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/1ca433e68fd2a57e9bd9666b76c0577fd84621eededde3a50d03a49723b21739.svg) the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
\left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(0,-1)} = -2(-1) = 2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Local Area Scale Factor of a Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $\Delta$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-1,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta{A}.$ Find an approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/ff668919204d7ccd57c1711fed961ca73562d47cc6f100511b06fe54a5ea212d.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\textrm{Area}\big(\mathbf{T}(\Delta)\big) \approx \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \cdot \underbrace{\textrm{Area}(\Delta)}_{\large \delta{A}}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{v}^{3} & 3u{v}^{2} \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={v}^{3}\cdot 2v-3u{v}^{2}\cdot 2u \\  & =2{v}^{4}-6{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-1,2)} & =(2{v}^{4}-6{u}^{2}{v}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-1\,v=2} \\  & =2(2)^{4}-6(-1)^{2}(2)^{2} \\  & =32-24 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|8|\cdot \delta A \\  & =8\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/57874e6e685ee9fb1a2b527fe046696aa983b04d22751c72d8a76783b349ca18.svg)

Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}  <    0
$$

We have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/4595adcbeb5ee3dc0bbe1258536e9b0e3e2fc81d5720a3394029df814f55f949.svg)

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{v} & u{e}^{v} \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{v}\cdot (-2v)-u{e}^{v}\cdot 2u \\  & =-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{v}({u}^{2}+v) & <0 \\ {u}^{2}+v & >0 \\ v & >-{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=-u^2
$$

defines a downward-opening parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Regions Where a Transformation is Orientation-Preserving or Reversing

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
We have explored linear and affine transformations in the plane. We'll now begin to explore nonlinear transformations of plane regions. 

Let  $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a **transformation** on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ We write
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/1137221ffc72c194aba941eaee899cc0a4134a92e92e86cfa65c88acd5f702ec.svg) 

Recall that, under this notation, 

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/0decb326ae66f97fb75a8df874479061fb1557b0437ca8ea1e7c5ed645db4b19.svg) represents vectors belonging to the input space (i.e., the $uv$-plane), and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/091b7a3ddf6ad7dc35360e728c2946481b3a17f60525d09676eb469ebd518a4d.svg) represents vectors belonging to the output space (i.e., the $xy$-plane).

For example, consider the following transformation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/239781240f2def3a5adf5331f36fa6dbdd3657ab431195c30cf3ede49d2ef3e2.svg) 

Geometrically, this transformation maps the rectangular region in the $uv$-plane below to a circular sector in the $xy$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/dcc80fe1271d560e9f958eba9454761d56f936567dc439853bc4181cccc3f76f.png)

We'll explore how to compute the image of a nonlinear transformation in future lessons. But for now, it is sufficient to know that 

- $\mathbf T$ takes points (or vectors) from the $uv$-plane as input and maps them to points (vectors) in the $xy$-plane, and

- rectangular regions in the $uv$-plane are mapped to regions in the $xy$-plane that are not necessarily parallelograms.

tutorials.name: The Jacobian Determinant
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it.

tutorials.title: The Jacobian Determinant
tutorials.content:
Suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) 

We'll assume that $\mathbf T$ is a $\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\Bbb R^2.$ 

The **Jacobian determinant** of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|=\frac{∂x}{∂u}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂v}-\frac{∂x}{∂v}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂u}\end{aligned}
$$

  

We sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**

Let's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) 

To compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it.

tutorials.name: A Review of Affine Transformations
tutorials.problem:
To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation 

$$
\mathbf x = T\mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf u, \mathbf b,$ and $\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. 

For an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:

- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:

If a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\det(T)|\cdot A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)

- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage.

If $\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)

- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*

If $\textrm{det}(T) \neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)

If $\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)

Affine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage.

tutorials.name: Intuition Behind the Jacobian
tutorials.problem:
The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

To understand what this means, suppose that $\mathbf{T}: U \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) 

and we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$

For ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$

$$
J(u_0,v_0) = \left.\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}
$$

Let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

- The *local* area scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\delta u$ and $\delta v,$ so its area is $\delta A = \delta u\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\left|J(u_0,v_0)\right| \cdot \delta A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)

Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0)\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)

If $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14142764/assets/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)

Points $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!
